National Assembly
National Assembly
Full Details of Proceedings
Thursday, August 14, 2083
Meeting Number - 38
The meeting of the National Assembly today commenced at 1:22 PM under the chairmanship of the Honourable Chairperson Mr. Narayan Prasad Dahal.
Honourable Chairperson: Honourable members,
(1:22 PM)
It has been decided to allocate one minute each for speaking during the Zero Hour. First, Honourable Member Ghanshyam Rizal.
Honourable Mr. Ghanshyam Rizal (Nepal Communist Party): Honourable Sir, the express vehicle, which had stopped earlier in front of the VIP entrance, was travelling in reverse gear. As the co-drivers were turning the steering wheel haphazardly, the vehicle is now attempting to make unauthorized entry and cause damage within the VIP compound, passing through the private residence of journalist Kishore Shrestha, who is also the chairperson. If the reverse gear is not corrected and proper direction is not given, an accident is certain. I urge all passengers on the express vehicle to be alert and demand the release of journalist Kishore Shrestha. Thank you.
Honourable Member Padam Bahadur Pariyar.
Honourable Chairperson: (1:23 PM)
Honourable Mr. Padam Bahadur Pariyar (Nepali Congress): Honourable Sir, while the 140 MW Tanahu Hydropower project is under construction in Tanahu district, the residents of Tanahu are as happy as they are, but the story of risk and suffering due to the negligence in this project, causing the Vyas-12 and Belbas areas of Tanahu to be submerged, is even more concerning. We are left wondering if we are rolling out the red carpet for destruction in the name of development. The natural flow of the Seti River has been altered without the consent of the local people during the construction of the Tanahu Hydropower project, forcing the residents of the surrounding areas to leave their natural homes and livelihoods. This has also led to increasing animosity between our own brothers on both sides of the river due to the project, and one local resident has even died. Therefore, I would like to draw the attention of the Government of Nepal, Ministry of Energy, to implement the report prepared by the ADB's Compliance Review Panel, which is a supporting body for this project. Thank you.
Honourable Chairperson: Honourable Member Rukmini Koirala.
(1:24 PM)
Honourable Ms. Rukmini Koirala (Nepal Communist Party, UML): (1:24 PM)
Honourable Chairperson, six Nepali mountaineers, including Nirmal Purja from Magdi, Gurung, Nawa Sherpa, Galjen Sherpa, Nawa Sherpa, and Kili Sherpa, lost their lives during the ascent of Broad Peak in the Karakoram region of Pakistan on August 2, 2083. I am deeply shocked by this sudden tragic incident. Three foreign nationals also died in this incident. I offer my heartfelt condolences to all the deceased. I also express my deep sorrow over the tragic murder of four promising young men in a religious conflict between Hindus and Muslims in Devangunj, Kapilgunj, Sunsari, on July 26. Honourable Chairperson: Honourable Member Renu Chand.
(1:26 PM)
Honourable Ms. Renu Chand (Nepal Communist Party): Honourable Chairperson, the victims of the reserve in Kanchanpur have been suffering for over two decades, and I wish to draw the government's attention to their plight. Thirty-one commissions and committees have been formed, and task forces have been established to study and recommend their resettlement. However, even after such a long time and so many commissions and mechanisms, the problems of the reserve victims have not been fully resolved. I urge the government to show immediate sensitivity to this issue and resolve the problem. Thank you.
Honourable Chairperson: Honourable Member Bishnu Kumari Sapkota.
(1:26 PM)
Honourable Ms. Bishnu Kumari Sapkota (Nepali Congress): Honourable Sir, the rent has become a major problem for low and middle-income citizens coming from remote areas to Kathmandu for employment and education. Income is limited, but rent is constantly increasing. Daily wage earners, students, employees, and small business owners have to spend a large portion of their income on rent. While the property rights of landlords must be protected, the practice of arbitrarily setting rent by taking advantage of the tenants' compulsion must also end. Therefore, my demand to the government is to immediately formulate a clear policy to regulate house and room rents in the Kathmandu Valley. A scientific rent should be determined based on the area, size, condition of the building, and facilities, and a maximum rent ceiling should be set in each area. Written agreements for house rent should be mandatory. Housing is a basic necessity for citizens; citizens who work in Kathmandu should not be in a situation where they cannot afford to live in Kathmandu. I wish to draw the government's attention to the immediate implementation of effective rent regulation laws and maximum rent rates. Thank you, Jai Nepal.
Honourable Chairperson: Honourable Member Bishnu Devi Pudasaini.
(1:28 PM)
Honourable Ms. Bishnu Devi Pudasaini (Nepali Congress): Honourable Sir, how can I begin to speak of scarcity? Protests and slogans are everywhere, when will they be fulfilled? There is a scarcity of gas, the kitchens of the people are closed, where has the government that chants slogans of good governance gone? Parents worry when their children go to school; they cannot even afford to give them hot water with noodles and biscuits. When the stove goes out in Singha Durbar and Baluwatar, everyone starts looking for a solution. Honourable Sir, I have presented all this hoping that the current government, which is a government of scarcity, might pay some attention. Thank you, Jai Nepal.
Honourable Chairperson: Honourable Member Bishnu Bahadur Bishwakarma.
(1:29 PM)
Honourable Mr. Bishnu Bahadur Bishwakarma (Nepal Communist Party): Honourable Sir, this government is causing suffering and deceiving the people by inciting students, instigating religious riots, chasing away the public, and now by reviving fake cases from the Maoist insurgency era. Just yesterday, Man Bahadur Bishwakarma, a resident of Ward No. 6, Narharinath Rural Municipality, Kalikot district, was arrested from his home in a kidnapping style without a warrant. The government should be warned; it will have to pay a heavy price. According to information received just now, he has been released. Man Bahadur Bishwakarma, who was arrested, has been released. Instead, the government should expedite the remaining tasks of the peace process through the Truth and Reconciliation Commission and the Commission of Mediation. With this, I conclude my remarks. Thank you.
Honourable Chairperson: Honourable Member Shrikrishna Prasad Adhikari.
(1:30 PM)
Honourable Mr. Shrikrishna Prasad Adhikari (Nepal Communist Party): Honourable Sir, the problems remain as they are. When prices fall in the international market, why is the domestic adjustment slow, as if unaware, but when prices rise, it is implemented immediately? What is the reason? The rampant price hikes and the artificial scarcity of cooking gas seen everywhere in the market have made the kitchens of ordinary people very expensive and difficult at this time. What concrete, exemplary plan is there to provide immediate relief to the public by increasing the storage capacity of the Oil Corporation, strict monitoring to control black marketing, ensuring easy availability of gas, and reducing the tax on fuel? I strongly demand from the government through this esteemed assembly for a clear answer. Thank you.
Honourable Chairperson: Honourable members, the order of speaking during the Zero Hour
(1:31 PM)
concludes here. Honourable members, names have been received on a party basis for speaking during the Special Time. Now I will provide time for Honourable members to speak. First, Honourable Member Bishnu Kumari Sapkota, time 14 minutes. Following this, Honourable Member Renu Chand.
Honourable Ms. Bishnu Kumari Sapkota (Nepali Congress): Honourable Sir, today, speaking of old parties and 35 years, leaders who fought for the rights and interests of the marginalized classes of Nepali citizens since 8 years ago, who today have given us rights as women, Dalits, and Janajatis, enabling us to stand tall, become Honourable members, and become ministers, these rights were given to us by those old leaders. Today, I want to remember those respected leaders of that time. The first people's representative Prime Minister BP Koirala (Bishweshwor Prasad Koirala), who faced eight charges of treason and was even threatened with his life, returned to Nepal at that time, setting aside his own life. On December 1, 2033 (BS), he returned to Nepal with a policy of reconciliation and national reconciliation and held talks with the then King Mahendra's government. That history is with us. Similarly, after the people's movement, the respected leader Sher Bahadur Deuba, who was injured, has been elected by the people, has served as Prime Minister five times, and has fought for democracy and constitutionalism, has returned to Nepal after his health treatment. I extend my heartfelt welcome and respect to him. Today, there has been a lot of upheaval in Nepal. It is not peaceful everywhere; there is scarcity; suicides are happening; depression problems persist; farmers have problems. There is a festival of problems; problems cannot be fully expressed. In the villages, and even in the cities, monkeys are causing so much trouble everywhere. No medicine, no control measures, no solutions for monkeys have been found. Similarly, in some places, wild boars, elephants, and rhinos are also causing trouble. Farmers are suffering from all sides; attacks are rampant. There is scarcity everywhere. On one hand, the Oil Corporation says it distributes 120,000 cylinders daily and delivers them to the market, while on the other hand, gas distributors say they cannot supply to 40 percent, only to 60 percent, and they cannot deliver. Wherever you go, the problem of gas is mentioned. Electricity is continuously increasing, but scarcity is also present; there are problems of frequent power outages. How will this be resolved? The government must play a coordinating role. Even to run a household, so much coordination and consultation are needed. To run this nation, it would be good to move forward by taking suggestions, opinions, and advice from political parties, civil society, intellectuals, and public representatives. However, the government does not seem to be engaged in that. Honourable Sir, the fundamental right to live with dignity, nutritious food, health, education, and freedom of expression, as guaranteed by the Constitution of Nepal, are all weakening, leading to an increase in depression and suicide rates day by day. Negative thinking is increasing among people. Where are our society, our religion, and our culture heading today? There is no dialogue between family members, no sharing of joys and sorrows; people feel lonely even in large groups. Cooperation, goodwill, and honesty towards each other are being severely misused in Nepal. It has imitated Western culture, and the mind is focused on abusive and negative matters. The government does not seem to be serious about this. This is a very sensitive issue; the government does not seem to be serious.

This is a very sensitive issue, so it should be a matter of concern for everyone. It is seen as necessary for the government to organize yoga, meditation, and spiritual practices from time to time for positive thinking and for the duty, loyalty, and responsibility towards the nation's citizens, including representatives of all three tiers of government – federal, provincial, and local – and all levels of employees. Because yoga, meditation, spiritual practice, and peace are our thousands of years old traditions. Nepal is not just a country of mountains, hills, and plains; Nepal is the land of penance for sages, enlightened yogis, and ascetics. Lord Buddha was born on this land, and numerous sages and practitioners have performed penance here. Our civilization is not just a story of physical development; it is also a story of human inner development.

Honorable Chairperson, Resunga in Gulmi and Shaligram Resunga and Virunga, the history of Shaligram is linked to the penance of Rishi Sringi and the spiritual practices of Rudra Devghat. On this sacred land, there is a tradition of penance and spiritual practice by practitioners like Mahaprabhu Lakshminarayan Swami, Bal Brahmachari Shashidhar Swami, Bal Brahmachari Chhabilal Swami, Bal Brahmachari Parmanand Swami, and Bal Brahmachari Yadukananda. Later, the arrival of great practitioners like Yogi Narharinath and their spiritual practices and life-giving herbs also connect Resunga to King Dasharatha and Shri Ram of Ayodhya. Similarly, Shalime Pond is not just a place of natural beauty and scenery, but also an important site connected to local religious beliefs, spiritual practices, and spiritual consciousness. The government should research and document the history and oral traditions of the saints and mahatmas who practiced spirituality in such places. We should not view such lands of penance merely as temples, ponds, or tourist spots. They should be developed as centers for yoga, meditation, silence, spiritual practice, spiritual tourism, and research.

Honorable Chairperson, today, stress, anxiety, unhealthy lifestyles, and social unrest are increasing worldwide. People have modern technology and facilities, but they are searching for peace of mind. In this situation, Nepal has a great contribution to offer the world: a balanced lifestyle based on yoga and meditation. It is positive that the government has started conducting yoga and meditation classes for government employees. But my request is: Let's not limit yoga to a program or a day; let's make it a national lifestyle. Let's practice yoga and meditation scientifically from schools to universities. Let's arrange regular yoga and meditation in government offices. Let's integrate yoga and meditation with health policy, tourism policy, and education policy. Let the government announce an ambitious national program. Let's create an international-level network of yoga, meditation, and spiritual tourism by connecting religious and spiritual sites like Nepal Yoga Meditation and World Peace Center Lumbini, Resunga Shaligram Daha, Pashupatinath, Muktinath, Janakpur, Halesi, etc. This will preserve our culture, create local employment, boost tourism, and give Nepal a new identity in the world.

Honorable Chairperson, the Himalayas are admired by the world. Buddha gave the message of peace to the world. Sages and hermits have shown the path of spiritual practice. Yoga teaches balance between body, mind, and consciousness. It has become necessary for the government to organize yoga, meditation, and spiritual practices from time to time for representatives of all three tiers and all levels, because it is now our responsibility to present these heritage sites to the world in a new way. Let's make Nepal not just a country people visit to see mountains, but a country where people come to seek peace of mind. Let's launch a national campaign to establish Nepal as a country of yoga, meditation, and world peace. This will be a true tribute to the sacrifice of our sages, enlightened great souls, and practitioners. Where there is the land of penance of Rishi Sringi in Resunga, and the tradition of spiritual practice of Mahaprabhu Lakshmi Narayan Swami and Shashidhar. Where there is the Siddha Yoga tradition of Gorakhnath and Machhendranath. Where Lord Buddha was born in Lumbini. Where practitioners like Yogi Narharinath enlightened Nepal's spiritual consciousness – this is our invaluable heritage.

Honorable Chairperson, since yoga, meditation, and spiritual practice are extremely important subjects connected to the life force of a person's body, mind, brain, and health, and given their unique identity, I want to draw the government's attention to establishing a separate policy, act, and law, and to advancing the process of opening and registering yoga practice centers as subjects for study, teaching, and experience.

Honorable Chairperson, through the Honorable Chairperson,

Today, for employees, there is a provision of working for 30 years and reaching the age of 54.

Chairperson,

Currently, the average lifespan of people has also increased. When the government retires employees who have worked for 30 years at the age of 44, has the government thought about what these employees will do after leaving their jobs at 44? I went to an office the other day, and a woman there said, 'I have become old. My energy to work is decreasing, but the government is telling me to leave at the age of 45. Today, I just realized I have become old. What will I do after this? It is very important to keep retired employees, who leave after the age of 55, engaged in some work. Because there are many jobs that can be created in Nepal. We have many products produced by our soil, but the government has not paid attention to them. Today, many of our youth have gone abroad. Today, the government, from yesterday to today, has been encouraging the sale of Nepali blood and sweat to foreign lands. Passports are still being made, but why can't we process and sell the herbs produced in our own country, on our own soil, instead of bowing down and begging from foreigners? What is the reason we need to be warned by foreigners, to be controlled by them? To do any work, one must take risks. Today, we are afraid to sell the things produced by our soil, but we are happily selling our youth power, our labor power; we are selling their sweat; we are enjoying the remittances earned by their blood and sweat. This should never be allowed to happen again.

Honorable Chairperson: Honorable Member Renu Chand, time 10 minutes.
(1:45 PM)
After this, Honorable Member Meena Singh Rakhal.
Honorable Shri Renu Chand (Nepal Communist Party): Honorable Chairperson,
(1:45 PM)
Sir, today I want to draw the government's attention to the incident that occurred in the Madhesh and Koshi provinces. This was a tragic incident in the name of religious fervor. And the firing that took place on the 23rd and 24th has once again stood before us. Who fired the shots? Government, who fired the shots? We need an answer. We need it immediately. And as soon as it starts in one place, it spreads across the country. We need information about what the government is investigating regarding how this dangerous thing is happening. The government has been late. It was the fifth day after the incident when the Home Minister went to the field. Although political actors, parties, religious leaders, journalists, and civil society appealed for cooperation, which was very helpful, the Prime Minister's address was delayed. He addressed, which is fine, but it cannot be said, 'better late than never.' My suggestion to the government is that swift action must be taken in sensitive incidents. In his address, he appealed for help from political parties, journalists, religious leaders, civil society, etc., which was good. But it doesn't work by banning; it doesn't work by prohibition. He must have learned the lesson that success is achieved with the help of society. He must have also learned the lesson that success is achieved with the cooperation of the global community, not by parking cars in front of gates. The report that was supposed to be submitted within 7 days should be presented to the House, because transparency is also a condition of good governance for the new government, and the public's right to be informed in the name of secrecy cannot be violated.

The fire has not been extinguished; the government should remain vigilant. Investments of a lifetime have turned to ashes; I demand that the state arrange compensation for them. Abuse continues at street corners, and inflammatory video messages are continuously being broadcast. The Ward Chairperson, who is the closest government representative, has not yet returned to the ward. There is a possibility of violence flaring up again at any time. Therefore, I want to seriously draw the government's attention to take immediate action against the culprits and manage the situation there.

And on another issue, I wasn't in the mood to speak about this repeatedly, but the minister himself asked yesterday why it wasn't done in 35 years, so I felt I should speak, and I want to tell the government that the question of 'What did you do in 35 years?' is being raised. The right to ask this question has been secured due to the sacrifices made within these 35 years. Where did you get the right to ask questions? We have to dig into history. You have now said not to ask questions, but in the past, asking questions meant losing your life, losing your head. The right to ask questions from there is a right won by fighting for these 35 years. Therefore, if anyone tells us not to ask questions now, we will not accept it.

And I want to present some facts to you. I want to specifically tell the government that in the 1991 census, Nepal's literacy rate was 39.6%; now in 2021, it is 76.2%. This is not just an increase in literacy; it is also a leap in consciousness. It should be understood in this way. Although the work of increasing skills and employment in schools and universities remains, you will do that. Nepal did not become poverty-free in 35 years, but Nepal's Human Development Index has increased from 0.395 in 1990 to 0.601 in 2022, an increase of 52.2%. This has happened in these 34 years. In 34 years, the country has journeyed from darkness to light, taking steps forward. The journey from being free from load shedding to electricity generation has been completed during the 35-year period. The right to speak, to assemble, and for us women, Dalits, and oppressed groups, the status of human beings has been achieved through the movement in these 35 years. These arduous 35 years have given us the pride of becoming citizens of a sovereign nation, moving from being subjects to sovereign citizens. I can provide more data, but time is short. What good work and progress have been made in the last 10 years has been publicly announced by the leader of the ruling party and the Finance Minister; please read that.

And I would like to appeal to the government side, the party in government, and the ruling side through the Honorable Chairperson that you are having a closed camp where you are training your ministers. Call Comrade Prachanda there, call the leader of the opposition party, we will also send our senior-most colleague from the National Assembly there. Give us a session there, and we will explain what we have done in 35 years.

This is my appeal to you. Because otherwise, you will ask these questions, you will know the answers, how many times will we answer? This will also facilitate political socialization and the exchange of experiences, which I see is greatly needed now. Now you answer, what have you done in these 4 months? What is the condition of the health insurance started by the old ones? Due to whom did Kedarnath Parajuli and his wife take Jal Samadhi? Who said that by sticking stickers, youth would be lured back to the country and given employment? From the Darar murder case to the Nimla Pant murder case, all issues...

With a snap of the fingers, we said 'Solve it,' or did you misunderstand? The government gives false assurances to the public, cannot fulfill them, and then scolds when questions are raised? What have you done for 35 years, burdening us with your incompetence? We will not carry your burden. It is astonishing that those who cannot even provide half a cylinder of gas to the public have the moral authority to ask us for an account of 35 years; this is truly astonishing. This has become like-

"They are busy digging through an ocean,
Busy finding our flaws.
Those whose own loincloths are torn,
Are busy taking off our turbans."

What kind of method is this? Don't get irritated after being questioned. We have been sent here by the public precisely to ask questions. You claim to be knowledgeable, technologically adept, and possess magical abilities, having come with the slogan 'The knowledgeable are chosen,' yet you now seek refuge by saying 'We are learning'? Clarify for us, is this newness your strength or your weakness? Because it is said 'The knowledgeable are chosen,' are you seeking leniency due to a lack of maturity, saying 'We are learning, we are studying'? You should not be given such excuses, and for how long will you be given special concessions for being new? We cannot give you special concessions for being new for much longer. In 35 years, we have written about health, education, and the right to live with dignity. We wrote it with great effort over 35 years. But what are you doing now? About 84 years ago, Yogmaya took Jal Samadhi (ritualistic self-immolation in water). After that, the political parties and activists of that time vowed that such a thing would never happen again. We have written many rights with great effort. Today, in your time, after almost 84 years, the Parajuli couple has taken Jal Samadhi. Who will take responsibility for this? Where are you misleading society? If you can, do better than the work we did in 35 years and move forward. Learn from our work, build upon it. Otherwise, the way despair is growing among the public and self-immolation attempts are increasing due to despair, and Jal Samadhi is being taken, this despair is the despair you have created. You will be entirely responsible for this; we will not carry this burden. Now what will you do? Tell us here. Will you pass a law for euthanasia? After failing to save people, will you give them the right to die voluntarily? What will you do? Give us the answer. Therefore, from now on, ask your leaders what happened and what didn't happen in 35 years; they will give you good training. If they don't, call us, and we will tell you. And please do not burden us with your own shortcomings; we will not carry this burden. This despair that is arising in society, people are ready to die by pouring petrol; is this a normal thing? A person is jumping into a river because their wife cannot get treatment; is this a normal thing? Your attention is not drawn to these matters. The danger of religious extremism is also increasing; your attention is not drawn to that, yet you get irritated as soon as questions are asked? We are the opposition with a clear mandate; the public has sent us to this parliament to ask questions, and we will ask questions. If you don't like it, that's your problem, but it is your responsibility to answer the questions raised by the public, by the people's representatives. You cannot evade that responsibility. We have no desire or wish to meet you personally and get answers. We will ask questions in the parliament, and you must answer here; you cannot deviate from your duty. Thank you. Honorable Chairperson: Honorable Member Meena Singh Rakhal, 10 minutes. (1:56 PM) After this, Honorable Member Puja Chaudhary. Honorable Mr. Minasingh Rakhal (Nepal Communist Party, UML):- (1:56 PM) Honorable Chairperson, thank you for giving me time. I will now turn to the government's 100-point agenda. The government's agenda, approved by the Council of Ministers on Chaitra 13, 2083, aims to make the overall performance of the government results-oriented, effective, measurable, and accountable, thereby directly improving citizens' lives. But the question is, where, how, and when have citizens received this result? And how do they feel they are receiving it? The government's first priority should be the security of citizens' homes and lives. However, actions like bulldozing landless squatters, making them homeless, and even demolishing temples and monasteries have not improved citizens' lives but have added fear and suffering. When will the squatters be managed? I want to ask, what is the government thinking? Chairperson, the incident where Bin Bahadur Rai was forced to commit suicide due to the unbearable bulldozer terror has questioned the government; why is this happening? Why is this occurring? Is the government a guardian of the citizens or a cause of displacement? On Saturday, April 12, 2072 (BS), an earthquake destroyed citizens' homes and caused loss of life and property. Similarly, on Saturday, April 12, 2083 (BS), this government bulldozed the squatter settlements. It is a tragedy that affected citizens have to face such terror and displacement from the government's bulldozers. It feels like this government is directionless. Therefore, the government's performance should not be measured by files and statistics, but by citizens' secure homes, dignified lives, and the feeling of justice. If the government is to be results-oriented, it must first provide secure shelter, not displacement. Chairperson, the government has announced the transformation of essential services like passports, citizenship, and driving licenses into a digital system to make them faster, easier, and more transparent for citizens. But the question arises here: citizens' suffering will never be alleviated by mere announcements, speeches, or Facebook statuses, nor can they be. Today, young men and women going to get passports are forced to stand in queues for hours outside and inside the offices, under the scorching sun and in the rain. Yesterday, it was said, 'You don't need to go abroad; passports will be delivered to your homes.' But today, the question for these youths is, 'The passport has been made, but where is the employment abroad?' Youth need opportunities to work with dignity in their own country, not passports and tickets to go abroad. While we talk about the government's digital system, why are service recipients still forced to endure crowds and hardship in queues? The situation at the transport office is similar. Thousands of service recipients are forced to stand in long queues for driving licenses. Due to the weekend holidays and staff shortages, citizens feel their time and labor are being wasted due to the inability to serve thousands of citizens. Chairperson, if the government is bringing a digital system, the system should be for the convenience of the citizens; citizens should not suffer due to the system's weaknesses. Therefore, through you, Chairperson, I draw the government's attention to immediately fill the staff shortage to take passport, citizenship, and driving license services fully into a well-managed digital system, manage the crowds, and arrange for services to be available even on public holidays if necessary. And the government's performance evaluation should be based not on announcements but on how long citizens have to wait in line to receive services. Chairperson, the government, society, and policy structures have committed injustices, discrimination, and deprivation against Dalits and historically marginalized communities. It was decided to issue a formal apology from the state and announce reformative programs within 15 days. But today, not just 15 days, but months have passed, and where has its concrete implementation reached? I want to ask the government a serious question: Deepa Nepali has been protesting at Maitighar Mandala for 116 days, saying 'The government has vacant rooms.' What is her health condition? Has the government been able to resolve the issue through dialogue, and what further programs are being planned? This is not just Deepa's issue; incidents like Dalits not getting rooms due to their caste, having to hide their surnames, facing violence and social boycott for inter-caste marriage, and being socially ostracized have come to light and are being witnessed. This is a matter of shame for our democracy. Despite inter-caste marriage being legally valid, violence and social pressure related to it are continuously seen. Reservation quotas for Dalits are necessary, but quotas alone are not social justice. Dalits must feel a tangible change in education, employment, land, housing, health, entrepreneurship, justice, and dignity. The demand from the government is to immediately implement the 15-day decision, examine Deepa's health, take legal action against those who discriminate in house rentals, and establish a special mechanism for the swift judicial resolution of discrimination against Dalits. The state must not only speak but also act. Chairperson, in Sunsari, citizens, including Gopal Yadav, lost their lives due to bullets in an agitation in the name of a religious community, but the responsible ministers of the state seemed to be merely fulfilling formalities rather than making citizens feel that the state exists. Why did Ganesh Nepali of Mugu, Karnali, reach the state of self-immolation by pouring petrol? Chairperson, the government has reached agreements with stakeholders multiple times, papers have been made. The Nepali family has not only lost their husband but also their means of sustenance. Signing papers does not wipe away the tears of the victims, nor does it light their hearths. My clear question to the government is, until when will you just make papers? When will you act? What is the deadline for fulfilling the commitments made to the victim's family? And will the state be present for the citizens' suffering, or will it only be on paper? I demand from the government that immediate steps be taken for their justice. Chairperson, sometimes, there may be disagreements with the subject matter of news reports. If a news report is perceived as incorrect, the path of legal recourse is open. However, arresting journalists based solely on writing or publishing a news report is a serious step against freedom of the press and the values of democracy. Journalism is the right to criticize and question, and the state using its power to imprison journalists simply because their criticism is disliked is unacceptable. I express my serious objection and strong protest against the arrest of journalist Kishore Shrestha. I strongly demand that this incident does not become a precedent for judicial and retaliatory behavior, that the legal process is respected, and that journalist Shrestha is immediately released to ensure the full guarantee of freedom. Thank you. Presiding Officer: Honorable Vice-Chairperson Lila Kumari Bhandari. (2:01 PM) Honorable Chairperson: Honorable Member Puja Chaudhary, 5 minutes. (2:06 PM) After this, Honorable Member Tul Prasad Bishwakarma. Honorable Mr. Puja Chaudhary (JSP, Nepal):- Honorable Chairperson, health services are guaranteed as a fundamental right by the constitution. However, in practice, for many Nepalis, falling ill still means weakening the family's financial condition, taking loans from others for treatment, being forced to sell land, and in some cases, being forced to abandon treatment altogether. According to World Health Organization (WHO) data concerning Nepal, approximately 24.9% face financial hardship due to out-of-pocket health expenditures. Currently, there is a shortage of vaccines and essential medicines even in government health institutions.

While not directly related to this bill, there was a time when Nepal Airlines had 22 aircraft and was profitable, and it owned land in many places in Kathmandu. We were profitable, and there is a history of expansion. Today, Nepal Airlines' liabilities exceed 56 billion, and it is incurring losses. The issue of how to revive it is certainly there. I am mentioning it because it was raised. Of the six aircraft brought from China, one met with an accident, and we have received the insurance amount for it. Four are remaining, but it is very difficult to operate them. The operational cost is very high, Nepali pilots cannot fly them, and their maintenance is very difficult and expensive, so they have been grounded. We need to think about this, but even though this is not related to this bill, I thank you for raising it. Similarly, Honorable Narayan Datta Mishra raised questions related to the issues of Sudurpashchim and Karnali. Some answers to these have been provided earlier. I believe I have explained the reasons why air travel is not possible in many remote hilly areas. The question of who is responsible for accidents is also important. Currently, there is a new concept of making others responsible, not the pilot, to prevent accidents. Ultimately, the entire responsibility for accidents is placed on the pilot, and they escape. A separate bill is coming regarding this, which will separate CAN into regulatory and service provider entities. These points will be included in that bill. However, this bill will also address some aspects. It will instill a sense of responsibility towards passengers in service providers. Therefore, I believe this will likely help reduce accidents. Regarding whether fare determination is transparent, I have already stated that fare determination in Nepal is linked to aviation fuel. A formula has been created for automatic adjustment of fares along with the increase or decrease in aviation fuel prices. However, it needs to be reviewed. It is a 10-15 year old formula, and it is still being applied. The issue of holding is a technical problem. All domestic air flights in Nepal are centered around Kathmandu. There is no significant holding problem elsewhere. Also, international flights arriving from abroad sometimes need to be given priority. Holding also occurs due to arriving at the last moment. We believe that after the successful implementation of this bill, issues like holding, flights not operating on time, and loss or damage of passenger luggage will be addressed. The concept of third-party insurance, which we call 'third party,' was not envisioned before. That is, if an aircraft crashes and falls on a house or community, there was a situation where the responsibility for the damage to other third parties was not to be taken, or there was no such clear law. There was no law at all. Therefore, this bill also addresses this. I believe all these things will help make Nepal's aviation more reliable and safer. I believe the queries of all honorable members have been addressed in a way. Thank you. Honorable Chairperson: Honorable members, the discussion on the proposal to consider the Domestic Air Service Liability Bill, 2083, is concluded here. Honorable members, I now present the proposal to consider the Domestic Air Service Liability Bill, 2083, for decision. Honorable members who are in favor of this proposal will say 'yes,' and those who are against it will say 'no.' Honorable members in favor of this proposal, say 'yes.' 'Yes.' Honorable members against this proposal, say 'no.' The sound of 'no' was not heard. Therefore, I declare that the proposal to consider the Domestic Air Service Liability Bill, 2083, has been unanimously approved. Honorable members, regarding the Domestic Air Service Liability Bill, 2083, I would like to inform those honorable members who wish to submit amendment proposals that they can register their amendment proposals at the legislative branch under the National Assembly, in accordance with Rule 106 of the National Assembly Rules, 2075. Honorable members, the next meeting of the National Assembly will convene on Monday, Bhadra 1, 2083, at 1:15 PM. This meeting is hereby adjourned.

The meeting was adjourned until Monday, Bhadra 1, 2083, at 1:15 PM. Adjourned: 3:54 PM.
